title: When climate and nature become security issues: risks and what the UK should do
label: 27 October 2026 · Climate diplomacy hearing
summary: Experts told the Foreign Affairs Committee that climate change and nature loss are rightly framed as national security risks because they threaten food, water, health, economies and stability; but they warned that calling them 'security' risks can push short-term, militarised responses unless the UK couples that framing with people-centred prevention, finance for adaptation, coalition-building at COP31 and clearer cross‑government roles.

chapters.title: Why call climate and nature 'security' issues?
chapters.takeaway: Experts agree the label helps elevate climate and nature loss to a political priority, but it must be paired with prevention and people-centred responses to avoid militarised short-termism.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should climate change and nature loss be treated as national security threats?

turns.speaker: Dr Mosello
turns.text: Yes. Calling them security issues stops them sitting in a single department. It shows they affect food, health, water and the economy, and so need system-wide government action and foreign policy attention.

turns.speaker: Laurie Laybourn
turns.text: I agree, but nature has been neglected compared with climate. We should think of an 'Earth system' threat—climate, water and biodiversity are linked and their failure threatens basic services like food.

turns.speaker: Janani Vivekananda
turns.text: I also agree with the framing, but worry about perception. If 'security' is left vague it can push militarised or short-term responses unless we deliberately pair it with adaptation, finance and people-centred policies.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the risk is that 'security' creates urgency but also invites the wrong kinds of action?

chapters.title: How security thinking could change responses
chapters.takeaway: Security actors are already involved, and some defensive or dual‑use measures (like restoring wetlands) can protect both security and nature, but we must avoid harmful securitisation.

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Security agencies already deal with environmental crimes. Some military assets are useful for disasters. There are 'dual-use' wins: restoring peatlands or wetlands can both trap carbon and act as physical defence.

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: But we should avoid a 'hard' security path like the problematic outcomes of the war on drugs. Stabilisation, diplomacy and peacebuilding are crucial responses too.

turns.speaker: Laurie Laybourn
turns.text: The challenge will be getting a progressive form of securitisation—one that raises priority but keeps focus on root causes like emissions and ecosystem collapse.

turns.speaker: Janani Vivekananda
turns.text: We must be explicit about what 'security responses' look like: more defence spending or emergency contingency planning would be the wrong emphasis unless matched by long-term prevention funding.

chapters.title: Food, migration and the regional hotspots
chapters.takeaway: Food and water stress, degraded soils and extreme heat will drive large internal movements, regional instability and economic shocks; hotspots include the tropics, parts of Africa, central Asia and heat‑vulnerable regions.

turns.speaker: Aphra Brandreth
turns.text: Should the UK treat domestic food production as a higher priority for national resilience?

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Yes. Globally we are losing viable agricultural land because of water stress, soil loss, pollinator declines and pests. That means people will either die, move or fight to secure resources.

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Countries are already buying food infrastructure abroad. That creates diplomatic complexity and points to the need for 'friendshoring'—building resilient, trusted supply chains.

turns.speaker: Edward Morello
turns.text: Do cuts to UK aid make migration and instability worse?

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Yes. Prevention is better. I ran a climate security project in Jordan that ended when UK funding stopped—losing programmes like that erodes local trust and capacity and can worsen crises and migration drivers.

turns.speaker: Sir John Whittingdale
turns.text: Which regions could become worst affected and drive mass movements?

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Maps and models point to equatorial regions—sub‑Saharan Africa, parts of central Asia and densely populated tropical zones by 2070. Estimates of total movement vary, but large-scale mobility is likely.

turns.speaker: Laurie Laybourn
turns.text: We must also factor in 'wildcards' like AMOC failing, which could unexpectedly shift who is vulnerable—even the UK could face severe climate shocks.

turns.speaker: Janani Vivekananda
turns.text: And lethal heat (high wet-bulb temperatures) is already hitting South Asia, parts of the Middle East and the Amazon; it reduces habitability and affects food production. Most movement so far is internal, not mass international migration.

chapters.title: Ranking threats and the economic picture
chapters.takeaway: For the UK the top concerns are large economic costs and impacts on investment, rising conflict and 'grey‑zone' tactics like lawfare and disinformation; these require both financial and diplomatic responses.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: Has anyone tried to rank these risks for UK priorities?

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Priorities vary by perspective, but for the UK economic costs are huge—studies suggest disruptions could amount to large fractions of GDP within decades. Conflict follows, and then 'grey zone' threats: information warfare, legal attacks and supply‑chain weaponisation.

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Insurance and investment patterns are already shifting, affecting capital flows and diplomatic relations when countries blame others for losses or extraction.

turns.speaker: Laurie Laybourn
turns.text: We must prepare for surprises and systemic cascading failures—it's not a single risk but interconnected problems that amplify each other.

chapters.title: What the UK should push at COP31, G20 and at home
chapters.takeaway: Experts want COP31 used for coalition-building on adaptation finance, disaster risk finance, resilient food systems and joint early-warning and risk assessments; domestically, clear departmental mandates and accountability are essential.

turns.speaker: Fleur Anderson
turns.text: Quickfire: what should UK priorities be at COP31 and as G20 chair?

turns.speaker: Janani Vivekananda
turns.text: Use COP for coalition-building—work with the EU, Kenya and African partners. At G20 focus on disaster risk finance, anticipatory action, debt treatment linked to climate resilience and climate-resilient food systems.

turns.speaker: Dr Mosello
turns.text: Adaptation and climate finance must be priorities. The UK hosts major private finance in the City—mobilising private capital for adaptation, and improving accessibility of finance to fragile and conflict-affected states, are vital.

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Preserve critical natural infrastructure—soils, wetlands, biodiversity corridors. Show practical wins and commit to implementation; leadership and clear messaging matter.

turns.speaker: Jessica Toale
turns.text: Is the UK's cross-government infrastructure for climate security joined up enough?

turns.speaker: Janani Vivekananda
turns.text: The taskforce is a good model and other countries are interested, but beware diffusion of ownership. Cross-government work needs specific, tangible mandates for departments so accountability isn't lost.

turns.speaker: Abtisam Mohamed
turns.text: How do we deal with ISDS and companies suing states over climate actions—can national security framing help?

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Lawfare is rising. The UK needs clear public red lines and coherent diplomatic positioning. Work with allies to shape norms and be consistent on energy and investment policy to reduce strategic risks.

turns.speaker: Laurie Laybourn
turns.text: The UK could define what it means by 'climate security'—a definition that protects domestic interests while enabling international cooperation—and then model mechanisms: assessments, alliances and early-warning research like AMOC monitoring.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the combination is: use diplomatic convening to build coalitions and finance, while at home give departments concrete roles and avoid turning security into only a hard, militarised response?

turns.speaker: Dr Mosello
turns.text: Yes — pair security framing with prevention: finance for adaptation, support for fragile states, and stronger water and food cooperation. That reduces the need for emergency, security-centred responses.

chapters.title: Practical steps and closing points
chapters.takeaway: Practical steps include sustained funding for prevention, clearer UK departmental mandates, coalition-building at COP/G20, investment in early warning and protecting food and water supply chains.

turns.speaker: Dr Clack
turns.text: Sustained programmes matter—projects stopped by funding cuts lose trust. Prevention and local capacity reduce migration and instability better than intermittent interventions.

turns.speaker: Laurie Laybourn
turns.text: Develop a British definition of climate security that commits to international cooperation; invest in early-warning and research collaborations with allies, especially on tipping points.

turns.speaker: Janani Vivekananda
turns.text: Institute departmental mandates, not just cross-cutting slogans. Translate climate security into concrete actions for MOD, Home Office, DESNZ and DFID-equivalent programmes so someone is accountable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. If you have further evidence, please write to us. This topic clearly requires urgent and joined-up policy—both at home and through diplomacy.
